t.7.9.1: Then, after some time, a Rākṣasa named Sumālī came up from Rasātala and roamed over the whole world of mortals.
t.7.9.2: Resembling a dark rain-cloud and wearing earrings of burnished gold, he took along his maiden daughter, who was like Śrī without her lotus, and then he saw Dhaneśvara travelling in the Puṣpaka.
t.7.9.3: Seeing him passing by, godlike in appearance and blazing like fire, the Rākṣasa then spoke to his daughter, who was called Kaikasī by name.
t.7.9.4: Daughter, this is the time for giving you in marriage, for your youth is slipping past. And on your account all of us, whose minds are set on dharma, are held in restraint.
t.7.9.5: For you, dear daughter, are endowed with every virtue, like Śrī herself holding her lotus; yet, fearing rejection, suitors do not seek your hand.
t.7.9.6: Being the father of a daughter is indeed a sorrow for all who care for their honour, for no one knows who will seek the maiden in marriage, my daughter.
t.7.9.7: The family of her mother, the family of her father, and the family into which she is given: a maiden always keeps these three families in a state of uncertainty.
t.7.9.8: Therefore, daughter, go yourself to Viśravas, the Paulastya, most eminent among the foremost of sages, born of the lineage of Prajāpati, and choose him of your own accord.
t.7.9.9: Your sons, O daughter, will without doubt be such as this lord of wealth is, equal to the sun in splendour.
t.7.9.10: Meanwhile, O Rāma, the twice-born son of Pulastya was attending to the agnihotra, shining like a fourth fire.
t.7.9.12: But he, most noble and seemingly blazing with energy, having looked upon her of shapely hips, whose face was like the full moon, spoke.
t.7.9.11: But she, out of reverence for her father's wish, gave no thought to that dreadful hour; she approached and stood before him, her face bowed down toward his feet.
t.7.9.14: Thus addressed, the maiden, with joined palms, then said: "O sage, by your own power you are able to know my intention."
t.7.9.13: Gentle lady, whose daughter are you, and from where have you come here? What is your purpose, and for whose sake have you come? Tell me truthfully, O lovely one.
t.7.9.15: But know, O brahmin, that I have come here at my father's command; Kaikasī is my name, and the rest you are able to know for yourself.
t.7.9.16: The sage, having entered into meditation, spoke these words: "I have understood, gentle lady, the reason that lies in your mind."
t.7.9.17: Since you have approached me at a dreadful hour, listen, good lady, to what kind of sons you will therefore bear.
t.7.9.18: O fair-hipped one, you will give birth to dreadful rākṣasas, dreadful in form, fond of dreadful kinsfolk, and cruel in their deeds.
t.7.9.20: Then the sage said there: "The last of your sons will be worthy of my lineage, and he will be righteous-souled."
t.7.9.19: Having heard his words, she bowed low and said: 'O blessed one, such sons are not fitting to be born of you, whose lineage springs from Brahmā.'
t.7.9.21: Thus addressed, O Rāma, that maiden after some time gave birth to a hideous and exceedingly dreadful being in the form of a Rākṣasa.
t.7.9.22: Ten-headed, with huge fangs, resembling a heap of dark collyrium, copper-lipped, twenty-armed, with a vast mouth and blazing hair.
t.7.9.23: Then, the very moment he was born, jackals with mouthfuls of flame and other flesh-eating creatures wheeled about in circles moving to the left.
t.7.9.24: The god rained blood, and the clouds thundered harshly; the sun did not shine in the sky, and great meteors fell upon the earth.
t.7.9.25: Then his father, equal to the Grandsire, gave him a name: "Since this one was born with ten heads, he shall be Daśagrīva."
t.7.9.26: Right after him was born Kumbhakarṇa of mighty strength, than whose dimensions no greater dimension is found in this world.
t.7.9.27: Then was born the one named Śūrpaṇakhā, of misshapen face, and Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous of soul, the last son of Kaikasī.
t.7.9.28: They, of exceedingly great might, grew up there in the great forest; and among them the cruel Daśagrīva became the one who brought terror to the worlds.
t.7.9.29: But the wicked Kumbhakarṇa, reckless and intoxicated, roamed about devouring the great sages devoted to dharma and terrifying the three worlds.
t.7.9.30: But Vibhīṣaṇa, righteous of soul, ever established on the path of dharma, dwelt there devoted to sacred study, restrained in his food, with his senses under control.
t.7.9.31: Then, after some time, the god Vitteśvara, lord of wealth, came there in the Puṣpaka to see his father of great splendour.
t.7.9.34: O Daśagrīva, my son of boundless valour, make such an effort that you may quickly become the equal of Vaiśravaṇa.
t.7.9.33: Son, behold your brother Vaiśravaṇa, enveloped in splendour; and though the bond of brotherhood is the same, look at yourself, how you are!
t.7.9.35: Having heard those words of his mother, the mighty Daśagrīva was seized by an unequalled indignation, and then he made a solemn vow.
t.7.9.36: I promise you truly, mother: before long I shall become equal to my brother, or even greater than him. Cast off the anguish that dwells in your heart.
t.7.9.32: Seeing him there, blazing as it were with splendor, Kaikasī, adopting a rākṣasa's way of thinking, spoke to Daśagrīva.
t.7.9.37: Then, driven by that very anger, Daśagrīva, together with his younger brothers, resolved, "I shall attain my desire through austerity," and, having firmly determined upon it, came to the auspicious hermitage of Gokarṇa for the sake of his own accomplishment.
